meta.title: Hebrew C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hebrew → English (see the Hebrew, recall the meaning) and English → Hebrew (see an English meaning, recall the Hebrew). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. The Hebrew taught is the modern standard language of Israel. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hebrew, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 60 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — philosophy and ethics, religion and Jewish tradition, scholarly Hebrew, government and the constitution, the economy and development, medicine and the body, law and rights, language and the forms of Hebrew poetry, the shades of feeling and judgement, the abstract nouns and adjectives of formal prose, and the literary connectors — and the other 1440 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hebrew, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, including the forms written with a prefix such as ו "and", ה "the" or ב "in" joined to the front. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hebrew is normally written — without vowel points, in the full spelling — with the POINTED form beneath it, which shows how it is said, and Wiktionary's romanisation with the stress marked (shalóm, katáv). Words spelt alike are separate cards where the level teaches both (שֵׁם "name", שָׁם "there"). The Hebrew Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters and the vowel points. The 971 nouns show their gender and plural; the 291 verbs are given, as Hebrew dictionaries give them, in the past tense "he" form, with their infinitive, present, future and binyan (the verb pattern) beside them and, behind the All forms fold, their past, present, future and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 1330 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 1034 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, pointing and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
